claims.claim: Fire and Blood doubles as a diegetic chronicle written by Maester Gyldayn whose in-world publication year is unclear.
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: The book's opening sentence assigns history-keeping to the maesters of the Citadel, implying historiography confined to an ivory tower, unfunded and unnoticed by rulers.
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: Contemporary fantasy assumes knowledge must be sought where it is hidden, and that the hidden truth may not in the end be trustworthy, so transmission itself is threatened.
claims.quote: might not, in the end, be trustworthy
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: In-world histories such as Daeron's Conquest of Dorne are remembered for their inaccuracy ('vainglorious', 'boastful'), and propagandistic history-writing has otherwise died out in Westeros.
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: The Kingsguard's White Book, a list of knights and deeds, echoes warrior chronicles such as Froissart's.
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: Deep time is hostile to book knowledge, and the loss of knowledge is the greatest challenge to fantasy realms concerned with the distant past.
claims.quote: Deep time is hostile to book knowledge
claims.page: Book Culture and Narrative in Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.feature: chronicle to reminiscence to fairy tale
claims.claim: The Harrenhal tourney exists in three registers: the World of Ice and Fire chronicle, scattered eyewitness reminiscences, and Meera Reed's fairy-tale retelling, tracing how history becomes tale.
claims.source: Bartlomiej Blaszkiewicz, 'From Chronicle to Fairy Tale', in Marchen und Gesellschaft (WUW, 2024), pp. 163-175
claims.quote: scattered personal reminiscences of various eyewitness characters

claims.feature: imitated chronicle style plus modern simplification
claims.claim: The real authors of The World of Ice and Fire imitated the style of the medieval chronicle and synthesized it with modern simplistic historical representations.
claims.source: Maksim Kyrchanoff (Kirchanov), Journal of Frontier Studies 2018 no. 1
claims.quote: imitated the style of the medieval chronicle
claims.page: Historical grand narratives of the Seven kingdoms of Westeros

claims.claim: The imagined author orders events chronologically and periodizes into named ages (Dawn Age, Age of Heroes, Long Night, Doom of Valyria), linear yet imagined as torn apart.
claims.source: Maksim Kyrchanoff (Kirchanov), Journal of Frontier Studies 2018 no. 1
claims.quote: imagined his "linear time" as torn apart
claims.page: Historical grand narratives of the Seven kingdoms of Westeros

claims.claim: The imagined chronicler allows himself estimates of the world's age ranging from 40 to 500 thousand years, a hedge of enormous width stated flatly.
claims.source: Maksim Kyrchanoff (Kirchanov), Journal of Frontier Studies 2018 no. 1
claims.page: Historical grand narratives of the Seven kingdoms of Westeros

claims.claim: Gyldayn's Dance history rests on three fictional primary sources: Septon Eustace, Maester Munkun, and the Testimony of Mushroom.
claims.page: Badgering on Mushroom: Historiography and Outsiders in House of the Dragon

claims.claim: Mushroom peppers his account with debauchery and ribald humor and is by far the most amusing of the three chroniclers.
claims.page: Badgering on Mushroom: Historiography and Outsiders in House of the Dragon

claims.claim: The device mirrors real premodern sources (Procopius, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Froissart), which are later compilations, paraphrases and unreliable narrators.
claims.quote: later compilations, paraphrases, and unreliable narrators
claims.page: Badgering on Mushroom: Historiography and Outsiders in House of the Dragon

claims.claim: Showrunner Condal says the show left the Rashomon-style telling to the book and instead defined an objective truth, which Mondschein calls a category error about real history.
claims.quote: we kind of left that to the book
claims.page: Badgering on Mushroom: Historiography and Outsiders in House of the Dragon

claims.claim: The narrator openly admits where the history gets muddled between Eustace's sober account and Mushroom's sensational one and leaves the reader to decide.
claims.page: House of the Dragon Misses One of the Best Aspects of Fire & Blood

verdicts.trueWording: “the extradiegetic book Fire and Blood … doubles as a diegetic chronicle, written by Maester Gyldayn, but its diegetic year of publication is unclear” (n.11, p.172).
verdicts.note: Raw PDF of the article (21 pp.) reached via Wayback capture 20251004113739id_ of dc.swosu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3342&context=mythlore (live viewcontent.cgi returns 403/AWS-WAF). Footnote 11 carries the quote word for word and supports Gyldayn's authorship and the unclear diegetic publication year.

verdicts.trueWording: “The opening sentence of Fire and Blood tells us about ‘the maesters of the Citadel who keep the histories of Westeros,’ suggesting that history writing is confined to the ivory tower and not encouraged, funded, or even much noticed by the political rulers of King's Landing.”
verdicts.note: Same PDF, p.172. Every limb present: opening sentence, maesters of the Citadel keeping the histories, ivory tower, not funded, not much noticed by rulers.

verdicts.trueWording: “knowledge must be sought where it is hidden … but that the ‘hidden truth’ might not, in the end, be trustworthy. In short, transmission of information is threatened.”
verdicts.note: Appears twice — in the Mythlore abstract (also visible on the live landing page dc.swosu.edu/mythlore/vol43/iss2/11/) and in the article's introduction. All three limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “a book still discussed for its inaccuracy: it is both called ‘vainglorious’ … and ‘boastful’ … Such propagandistic use of history writing, however, seems to have died out.”
verdicts.note: PDF p.173. Both epithets and the death of propagandistic history-writing are on the page; the article hedges with ‘seems to have died out’ where the claim states it flatly, and Conquest of Dorne is the article's single example rather than a class of ‘histories’ — a modality/scope softening, not an unsupported limb.

verdicts.trueWording: “Jaime Lannister writes in the White Book, a list of Kingsguard knights and their deeds”; n.12 “The White Book bears echoes of the warrior chronicles of, for example, Jean Froissart.”
verdicts.note: PDF p.172 body plus footnote 12. Both limbs (list of knights and deeds; Froissart echo) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “Deep time is hostile to book knowledge, and it is the loss of knowledge that poses the greatest challenges to fantasy realms so concerned with the distant past.”
verdicts.note: Abstract wording, on the live landing page and in the PDF abstract; the body varies it slightly (‘but it is the very loss, or disappearance, of knowledge’). Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “the chronicle The World of Ice and Fire, which reappears in the form of scattered personal reminiscences of various eyewitness characters … to Meera Reed's fairy-tale version”
verdicts.note: Source reached is the CEEOL chapter-detail page itself (HTTP 200, publisher abstract; chapter PDF is paywalled at 6.50 EUR). The abstract carries the quote verbatim, names all three forms — chronicle, eyewitness reminiscences, Meera Reed's fairy tale — and states the aim as illustrating ‘the transformation of historical events into a fairy tale’. Caveat of record: the abstract frames the reminiscences as the chronicle narrative reappearing, so ‘three registers’ is the claimant's enumeration; the chapter body was not reachable.

verdicts.trueWording: “the real authors of the text actually imitated the style of the medieval chronicle, synthesized it with modern simplistic historical representations.”
verdicts.note: Full English text obtained from the article's own galley PDF (jfs.today/index.php/jfs/article/download/34/31/, linked from the given landing page), p.26. ‘The text’ is The World of Ice and Fire, the article's stated object of analysis.

verdicts.trueWording: “imagined his ‘linear time’ as torn apart … classification of events in their chronological order and sequence … ‘the Dawn Age’, ‘the Age of Heroes’, ‘the Long Night’, … ‘the Doom of Valyria’.”
verdicts.note: Galley PDF pp.26-27. All four named ages appear in the article's longer list of nine stages; chronological ordering and the torn-apart linearity are both stated.

verdicts.trueWording: “the imagined author of the historical chronicle allowed himself reasoning about the age of the world and his estimates ranged from 40 to 500 thousand years.”
verdicts.note: Galley PDF p.26. The figures and the flat, uncommented statement are on the page; ‘a hedge of enormous width’ is the claimant's gloss on the quoted range, not the article's phrasing.

verdicts.trueWording: “Gyldayn's history … is based on fictional primary sources: … a septon (priest) named Eustace; a Maester (academic) named Munkun; and the Testimony of Mushroom”
verdicts.note: Live page fetched 200 with a browser UA. ‘three fictional accounts’ also appears verbatim two paragraphs later; the history is explicitly the Dance of the Dragons account by Archmaester Gyldayn.

verdicts.trueWording: “Of the three fictional chroniclers, Mushroom is by far the most amusing, peppering his account with debauchery and ribald humor.”
verdicts.note: Same page; both limbs are one sentence of the source.

verdicts.trueWording: “So much of the information we have about the premodern world comes from later compilations, paraphrases, and unreliable narrators” — then Procopius, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Froissart.
verdicts.note: Same page. The three real analogues follow the quoted sentence in order, each with its unreliability named (Procopius' grudge, the ‘convoluted’ Chronicle, Froissart compiling events he did not witness).

verdicts.trueWording: Condal: “we kind of left that to the book, and decided to, instead, try to define what we thought the objective truth of this actual history was”; Mondschein: “there is no such thing as ‘actual history’ or being ‘right’ or ‘wrong.’”
verdicts.note: Same page; the quote is attributed there to showrunner Ryan Condal via a Polygon interview. ‘Category error’ is the claimant's label for Mondschein's rebuttal — he does not use the phrase, but he argues exactly that objective truth/right/wrong do not apply to real history.

verdicts.trueWording: “The narrator admits that the history gets muddled between Maester Eustace and Mushroom's accounts”; “the book leaves it to the reader to determine how much they want to believe.”
verdicts.note: Live Nerdist page fetched 200. Eustace's account is called ‘a sober recollection’ and Mushroom's ‘deeply sensationalized’. Minor agent shift: the source credits the book (with the narrator unsure) for leaving the choice to the reader; Nerdist also miscalls Eustace a Maester rather than a septon, which the claim does not repeat.
